title: Orbital Designation Matrix and the Spin Quantum Number
notes: How (n, l, m) triples map onto orbital designations, and what the spin quantum number adds — including the box-and-arrow notation used in configuration questions.
• l = 1 → p, 3 orbitals (m = −1, 0, +1): 2p, 3p, 4p … each written px, py, pz.
• l = 2 → d, 5 orbitals (m = −2 … +2): 3d, 4d … (dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y², dz²).
The full designation combines n and the subshell letter (3p) or, fully, (n, l, m) — e.g. (3, 1, 0) is the 3pz orbital.

mₛ = +½ (↑) or −½ (↓). Electron spin is an intrinsic angular momentum with magnitude √(3/4)·h/2π = √3/2 ħ — it is not literally a spinning ball, but the name survives. Evidence: Stern–Gerlach (silver atoms split into two beams) and doublet structure of alkali spectra. With spin, each orbital (defined by n, l, m) holds exactly two electrons of opposite spin — Pauli's exclusion principle.

Draw one box per orbital; fill per Aufbau/Pauli/Hund. Nitrogen: 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ (three boxes, parallel arrows); oxygen: 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑. The notation encodes unpaired-electron counts, hence magnetic behaviour: N has 3 unpaired (paramagnetic), Ne has 0 (diamagnetic).
Count unpaired electrons u: spin-only magnetic moment μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM. Fe³⁺ (3d⁵): u = 5 → μ ≈ 5.92 BM; Cu²⁺ (3d⁹): u = 1 → 1.73 BM; Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰): u = 0 → diamagnetic.
confusion: ❌ Spin means the electron literally spins on its axis. ✅ Spin is an intrinsic quantum property; the classical picture is only an analogy.
❌ The five d orbitals have five different energies in a free atom. ✅ They are degenerate; ligand or magnetic fields split them.
❌ A full designation needs only n and l. ✅ A complete state needs all four numbers (n, l, m, mₛ).

universalFacts: The five d orbitals carry the spectroscopic labels dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y², dz².

Pauli stated his exclusion principle in 1925, before spin was formally introduced.
examples: **Problem:** Give the designation of an electron with (n, l, m, mₛ) = (4, 2, −1, +½). **Solution:** n = 4, l = 2 → 4d; m = −1 selects one of the five d orbitals; mₛ = +½ — an up-spin electron in a 4d orbital.

Pauli's principle is stated in terms of the four quantum numbers — quote all four.

summary: The quantum-number triple (n, l, m) maps onto orbital designations in a fixed matrix: l = 0 gives s with one orbital (m = 0) as 1s, 2s, 3s; l = 1 gives p with three orbitals (m = −1, 0, +1) as 2p, 3p, written px, py, pz; l = 2 gives d with five orbitals (m = −2 … +2) labelled dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y² and dz²; l = 3 gives f with seven orbitals (m = −3 … +3). A full designation combines n and the letter (3p), and the complete state (3, 1, 0) is the 3pz orbital. Spin adds mₛ = ±½, an intrinsic angular momentum of magnitude √3/2 ħ rather than a literal spinning ball, evidenced by Stern–Gerlach and the alkali doublets; with spin each orbital defined by n, l and m holds exactly two opposite-spin electrons, which is Pauli's exclusion principle in this language.
importantConcepts: Designation matrix: l = 0 → s (1 orbital), l = 1 → p (3), l = 2 → d (5), l = 3 → f (7)
m values run −l to +l, so the triple (n, l, m) fixes a single orbital, e.g. (3, 1, 0) is 3pz
d orbitals carry the spectroscopic labels dxy, dyz, dxz, dx²−y² and dz²
Spin: mₛ = ±½ with intrinsic angular momentum √3/2 ħ, evidenced by Stern–Gerlach (silver splits into two beams) and doublet spectra
With spin, each orbital holds exactly two electrons of opposite spin — Pauli's exclusion principle; box notation shows ↑ ↑ ↑ before ↑↓
importantStatements: Spin is an intrinsic quantum property, not a classical rotation, though the name survives.
The five d orbitals are degenerate in a free atom and split only in ligand or magnetic fields.
A complete state needs all four numbers; n and l alone describe a whole subshell.
Silver's single unpaired 5s electron produced exactly two Stern–Gerlach beams, confirming s = ½.
Pauli stated his exclusion principle in 1925, before spin was formally introduced.

keyPoints: Orbitals per subshell 2l + 1; capacity 2(2l + 1): s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.
Box notation: one box per orbital, parallel arrows first (Hund), opposite arrows only when paired (Pauli).
μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM: Mn²⁺ (u = 5) gives 5.92 BM, Cu²⁺ (u = 1) gives 1.73 BM, Zn²⁺ (u = 0) is diamagnetic.
Nitrogen 2p³ has three unpaired electrons, oxygen 2p⁴ has two.
specialNotes: Degenerate orbitals split in a magnetic field — that is the Zeeman effect in matrix language.
A subshell is (n, l); an orbital is (n, l, m); an electron state adds mₛ.
Box arrows represent mₛ only; the orbital shape comes from l and never changes with spin.
examShortTricks: Use box notation whenever unpaired electrons or magnetism are asked — it is faster and safer.
State Pauli's principle in terms of all four quantum numbers, not just 'two per orbital'.
(3, 1, 0) = 3pz; (4, 2, −1) = one of the five 4d orbitals — this mapping is a favourite one-mark item.
